sections.title: Primary and Secondary
sections.html:
The Sages said: "This is the rule: whenever there is a primary food (ikar) accompanied by a secondary one (tafel), one recites the blessing over the primary and exempts the secondary" (Berakhot 44a). To what may this be compared? To a person who received from his friend a gift wrapped in beautiful paper: it is fitting that he give thanks for the gift, and included in the thanks for the gift is thanks for its lovely wrapping. If he were to give thanks for the wrapping paper by itself, he would thereby express that he did not understand what the gift is, or that it is unimportant in his eyes, to the point that he equates it with its wrapping. Likewise, for one who eats a primary food accompanied by a food that is secondary to it, the Sages instituted that he recite the blessing over the primary food and thereby exempt the food secondary to it. However, it must be defined when a food is secondary to another and when it is not, and in order to understand the halakha well, we will mention many examples in this chapter:

If he had on his plate fish, ptitim and potatoes, since each of the foods has importance of its own, he recites over each one its blessing: over the ptitim Mezonot, over the potatoes Ha-adama, and over the fish Shehakol. Even though the fish is more important to him, and even though he intends to eat them literally together, they are not considered secondary to the fish, and therefore he must recite over each food its blessing. Likewise, at the end he recites Al Ha-miḥya over the ptitim, and Borei Nefashot over the fish and the potatoes.

But if he had on his plate ptitim and beside them an accompaniment intended to flavor them, such as ketchup, teḥina, hot sauce (skhug), eggplant salad or matbuḥa, he recites Mezonot over the ptitim and exempts the accompaniments beside them. For the whole purpose of the accompaniments is to flavor the ptitim, and were he not eating the ptitim, he would not eat the accompaniments. However, if he wants to taste the ketchup or the teḥina by themselves, in order to enjoy their taste, he will have to recite Shehakol over them. But when the ptitim are primary and the ketchup and teḥina are secondary to them, he recites the blessing over the ptitim and exempts the accompaniments.

If, after reciting the blessing over the ptitim, he went and recited a blessing over one of the accompaniments, his blessing is in vain, because the accompaniments were already exempted by the blessing he recited over the ptitim. And if before reciting the blessing over the ptitim he recited a blessing over the accompaniments – for example, he first recited Shehakol over the ketchup – although this does not involve the severe prohibition of a 'berakha le-vatala' (a blessing in vain), since he had not yet recited the blessing over the primary food and consequently had not yet exempted the secondary one, nevertheless it involves the prohibition of a 'berakha she-eina tzerikha' (an unnecessary blessing). That is, it is a superfluous blessing, for with the blessing he is about to recite over the ptitim, which are primary, he will exempt the accompaniments meant to flavor them (SA 212:1; MB 168:48; 215:18).

Even if, after he finishes the ptitim, a little of the accompaniments remains on his plate and he wants to eat it, he should not recite a blessing over it, for since it was secondary to the ptitim, it was exempted by the blessing he recited over the ptitim. But if a lot of the accompaniments remains and he wants to eat them because of their taste, their eating has independent importance, and he must recite a blessing over them (MB 168:46).1

Even bread can, on rare occasions, be considered secondary. For example, one who wants to drink a strong alcoholic drink and, to dull its sharpness, eats bread with it – since the drink is primary, he recites the blessing over it and exempts the bread. But if he also wanted to be satiated by the bread or to enjoy its taste, even though his main aim is to drink the beverage, since he is also interested in the bread, because of its importance it becomes primary, and with the Ha-motzi blessing he recites over the bread he also exempts the drink (SA 212:1; MB 5; and see above 3:6).

sections.title: When There Is a Doubt Whether One Food Is Secondary to Another
sections.html:
One who eats kugel with a pickled cucumber: if it is clear to him that the cucumber is secondary to the kugel, because the whole aim of eating it is to flavor the kugel, then with the Mezonot blessing he recites over the kugel he exempts the cucumber. But if he is in doubt – perhaps the cucumber has independent importance, for although without the kugel he would not eat it, and thanks to the kugel he enjoys it more, nevertheless in practice he enjoys it in its own right, and therefore he will also want to taste it by itself – in such a case he should first eat a little of the kugel by itself and recite Mezonot over it, and a little of the cucumber by itself and recite Ha-adama over it, and afterward continue eating them together.

This is the proper practice in any case where a doubt arises whether a certain food is secondary to another: he should first recite a blessing over each food separately and eat a little of it, and thereby get out of the doubt, and afterward he can continue eating both together. There is no concern of a 'berakha she-eina tzerikha' in this, since it is needed in order to get out of the doubt (Pri Megadim; Sdei Ḥemed).2

Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate them together, even though he ate a kezayit of each of them, he recites only Al Ha-miḥya, for since he is in doubt whether the cucumber is important in its own right, he cannot recite a blessing over it. In order to get out of the doubt, it is good that he eat or drink something else that will obligate him in the Borei Nefashot blessing. Likewise, if he eats a kezayit of the cucumber separately, he will become obligated to recite Borei Nefashot over it.

sections.title: A Mixture of Two Kinds
sections.html:
Many foods are composed of different kinds of food which, had they been eaten separately, would each have required its own special blessing; but since they were mixed together they became one food. With respect to the blessing, the central food in the mixture is the primary one, and the other foods become secondary to it and are exempted by its blessing. For example, rice into which raisins or tuna were mixed: since the rice is primary, he recites Mezonot over it and exempts the raisins and the tuna. Likewise, one who eats a vegetable salad into which a few pieces of olive were mixed in order to add flavor to it – since the vegetables are primary, he recites Ha-adama over the salad and exempts the olives. Likewise, rice on which almonds were placed in order to beautify and flavor it: the almonds are secondary to the rice, and the Mezonot blessing he recites over the rice exempts the almonds.

When both kinds in the mixture are important and completely mixed together, one follows the majority. For example, if a pashtida was made of cheese and vegetables: if the majority is vegetables, its blessing is Ha-adama, and if the majority is cheese, its blessing is Shehakol. Likewise, if rice and lentils were mixed: if the majority is rice, one recites Mezonot, and if the majority is lentils, one recites Ha-adama. Likewise, if yogurt and pieces of fruit were mixed: if the majority is yogurt, its blessing is Shehakol, and if the majority is tree fruit, its blessing is Ha-etz.3

However, when the pieces in the mixture are recognizable, as in a fruit salad that contains pieces of tree fruits and pieces of fruits of the ground, since the pieces are relatively large and it is recognizable from which fruit each of them comes, there is a doubt whether the blessing over the majority exempts the minority. Therefore one should first take a piece of tree fruit and recite Ha-etz over it, and a piece of fruit of the ground and recite Ha-adama over it, and afterward continue eating them together.4

sections.title: A Mixture Containing a Grain Species
sections.html:
As we have learned, in an ordinary mixture one follows the majority, but if one of the kinds that make up the mixture is of the five species of grain, its blessing is Mezonot. For example, a cake, even though most of its ingredients are sugar, eggs, nuts and chocolate, if it contains flour from the five species of grain, its blessing is Mezonot. Likewise, a vegetable pashtida into which a little flour was mixed in order to improve its taste – the flour is primary, and one recites Mezonot over the pashtida. This is because the five species of grain are the most important of foods, from which bread and Mezonot are made; therefore, whenever they are present in a mixture, they determine the blessing. The same applies to a noodle and cabbage salad: since a grain species is mixed into the salad, even when the grain is the minority, its blessing is Mezonot.

All this is on condition that the grain is intended to give flavor to the food or to satiate; but if the role of the grain is to bind the ingredients of the cooked dish or baked good, the grain is secondary to the other ingredients and does not have the power to determine the blessing. Therefore, over a vegetable pashtida into which flour was mixed in order to bind the pashtida, one recites Ha-adama (SA 208:2-3). A fish or meat patty into which breadcrumbs were mixed in order to increase its volume and make it soft – the breadcrumbs are secondary to the meat or fish, and one recites Shehakol over the patty (Avnei Nezer OḤ 38).5 In a case of doubt, a person must decide according to his understanding whether the purpose of the grain is for flavor or for binding and the like.

Sometimes there is a doubt whether the food before us is one food containing several ingredients, so that one must recite the blessing over the primary and exempt the secondary, or a combination of several foods over each of which one must recite a blessing separately. For example, ḥamin (cholent with dough) that contains groats, a flour pudding [?] (kugel), pieces of potato, beans and meat. Even when the flour pudding has crumbled and spread throughout it, there is still a doubt whether the ḥamin is considered one mixture and its blessing is Mezonot, or whether the pieces of meat and potato are considered separate kinds, because they are recognizable, and one must recite over them their blessings. As we have learned (halakha 3), in such a situation one should first recite a blessing over each food separately: over the groats Mezonot, over a potato Ha-adama, and over a piece of meat Shehakol, and afterward eat the ḥamin as a mixture.

Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate a kezayit of the grain species, he recites Al Ha-miḥya. Regarding the other kinds, if they were completely mixed, so that he did not eat a kezayit of them separately, because almost always he also lifted some of the grain species with his fork, there is a doubt whether he should recite Borei Nefashot over them, for perhaps they were exempted by the blessing over the grain. But if he ate a kezayit of them separately, that is, in the total of all the times he ate them alone there was a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot. Likewise, if the grain he ate did not amount to a kezayit, and the other foods amounted to a kezayit, even though they were mixed, he recites Borei Nefashot (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 212:2).

sections.title: Additional Foods (Schnitzel, Kubbeh, Strudel, Stuffed Pepper, Moussaka)
sections.html:
Over chicken or fish schnitzel one recites Shehakol. Although its coating contains grain that adds flavor, since it is not mixed into the food, and its aim is only to flavor the meat from the outside, the meat remains primary. Likewise, fried eggplants coated in flour or breadcrumbs – their blessing is Ha-adama (this is the custom. And even according to those who hold that their blessing is Mezonot, since there is a doubt in this, they must recite Shehakol).

But over kubbeh, which is a patty that has a thick casing of dough with meat inside it, since the dough has independent importance, it is primary, and therefore its blessing is Mezonot.

Likewise, over a strudel filled with meat, since the casing of dough baked together with the filling has independent importance, even though it is thin and small relative to the meat, the dough is primary, and the blessing over the whole strudel is Mezonot. At the end, if the dough amounted to a kezayit (half an egg), he recites Al Ha-miḥya. And if the dough did not amount to a kezayit but together he ate a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot. And if from the outset he wanted to separate the Mezonot casing of the strudel from the meat, he has turned it into two foods, and he recites a blessing over the Mezonot separately and over the meat separately, both the first blessing and the after-blessing.

Blintzes (ḥavitiyot), which are made of thin batter prepared in a frying pan and filled with cheese or mashed vegetables – even when the dough was not fried together with the filling, as long as he does not wish to separate the casing from the filling, this is one food, and consequently the dough is primary and its blessing is Mezonot (regarding the after-blessing, its law is like that of strudel).

'American peanuts' are peanuts coated in a thick layer of sweetened flour [batter]; since the flour is one of the ingredients of the food, its blessing is Mezonot. If he ate a kezayit of the flour coating alone, he recites Al Ha-miḥya at the end. And if he did not eat a kezayit of the flour, but of the two ingredients together he ate a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot.

There are foods about which it is difficult to determine whether there is a primary and a secondary among them, such as moussaka, which is a dish made of eggplant slices stuffed with minced meat; since both of its ingredients are important and recognizable, it is difficult to determine which of them is more important. Therefore he should first eat some of the eggplant alone and recite Ha-adama, and eat some of the meat alone and recite Shehakol, and afterward eat them together.

Over a pepper stuffed with rice and a little meat, one recites Mezonot, because the rice is primary, the role of the pepper is to wrap it and the role of the meat is to flavor it. If he separated the filling from the pepper in order to eat each of them separately, he recites Mezonot over the filling and Ha-adama over the pepper.

sections.title: A Cracker and What Is on It
sections.html:
One who spreads cheese or hummus on a matzia (a crispbread), a roll or a cracker, even if he spread a thick layer, as long as the spread is meant to flavor the baked good, even though he likes the spread very much, it is secondary to the baked good. He should recite Mezonot over the baked good at the outset and exempt the spread; likewise at the end, if he ate a kezayit of the baked good, he recites Al Ha-miḥya and exempts the spread. And if he did not eat a kezayit of the baked good, but the two together amount to a kezayit, since the spread is secondary to the baked good, they are considered one food containing a kezayit, and he recites Borei Nefashot, which is a more general blessing. The same law applies if he placed sausage on the baked good in order to flavor it (Da'at Torah 212:1; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 2).

But if he wants to eat the sausage for its own sake, and he places it on the baked good because it tastes better to him to eat both together, neither of them is secondary to the other. He should first recite Mezonot and eat some of the baked good, and afterward recite Shehakol and eat some of the sausage, and continue eating both together. The same law applies if he wanted to eat the baked good with a piece of fish or with a lot of cheese or vegetables: if he wants to eat each of them in its own right, he recites a blessing over the baked good separately and over what he wants to place on it separately, and afterward eats them together (MB 212:6; 168:45).

Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate a kezayit of the baked good and a kezayit of what was on it, even though he ate them together, since neither of them is secondary to the other, and they were not baked together, they are like two foods, and at the end he recites Al Ha-miḥya and Borei Nefashot. And if neither of them amounted to a kezayit, even though together they amount to a kezayit, since they are not one food, he does not recite an after-blessing (above 10, note 14).

Also when he is in doubt whether the food added to the baked good is secondary to it, he should first recite a blessing over the baked good separately and over the additional food separately, and afterward eat them together. There is no concern of a blessing in vain in this, since from the outset he intended not to exempt the additional food with the blessing he recited over the baked good (see note 2). Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate the measure of a kezayit of the baked good, he recites Al Ha-miḥya, and over the additional food he does not recite Borei Nefashot, since perhaps it was exempted by the Al Ha-miḥya blessing. Only if he eats a kezayit of the addition separately does he also recite Borei Nefashot. Likewise, if the baked good did not amount to a kezayit, and the additions amounted to a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot.

sections.title: Various Cakes, Ice Cream in a Cone, and Krembo
sections.html:
A cake that has a fruit or vegetable filling (strudel, a rolled pastry, pie): since the dough and the filling were baked together, it is one food, and since it contains grain species, even if the grain is the minority it is primary, and therefore one recites Mezonot over the cake. Likewise, a cake whose base is dough with slices of fruit on top: since everything was baked together, it is one food, and its blessing is Mezonot. For the after-blessing, if he ate a kezayit of the dough, he recites Al Ha-miḥya over the cake. And if he did not eat a kezayit of the dough, but together with the filling he ate a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot (see above 10, note 14).

But if they first baked a base of dough, and on it placed whipped cream, ice cream, cheese or jelly, if what was placed on the dough is substantial, since they were not baked together, what was placed on the dough also has independent importance, and therefore one must recite two blessings over this cake (MB 168:45). Likewise with the after-blessing, he recites over each of them separately: over a kezayit of the dough, Al Ha-miḥya, and over a kezayit of what is on top of it, Borei Nefashot.

Ice cream in a cone made of grain species: if from his perspective the cone is secondary, and its whole purpose is to hold the ice cream, he recites Shehakol over the ice cream and exempts the cone. But if he is interested in the taste of the cone, the cone too has importance, and therefore one must recite a blessing over both the ice cream and the cone. In terms of the order of precedence, it is preferable to recite Mezonot over the cone first, but when it is not convenient to begin eating from the cone, he should first recite Shehakol and eat some of the ice cream, and when he reaches the cone, recite Mezonot and bite from the cone. At the end of the eating he recites Borei Nefashot (and if he estimates that he ate a kezayit of the cone, he also recites Al Ha-miḥya; see above 10:11).

Krembo: since both the cream and the biscuit beneath it have importance, one should recite Shehakol over the cream and Mezonot over the biscuit. At the end, he recites Borei Nefashot over the cream, and over the biscuit he does not recite a blessing, since it does not amount to a kezayit (half an egg).

But over large ice cream rolls [?] made of Mezonot with ice cream inside them, since the Mezonot wraps the ice cream, they are one food, and one recites Mezonot over them. At the end, if he ate half an egg's volume of the Mezonot, he recites Al Ha-miḥya and exempts the ice cream. And if he ate less of the Mezonot, but together he ate half an egg's volume, he recites Borei Nefashot.6

sections.title: Sweets
sections.html:
Sugar-coated peanuts, and likewise chocolate-coated almonds: the primary component is the peanut or the almond, and the coating is meant to flavor it, and one recites Ha-adama over the peanut and Ha-etz over the almond. Over a candy that has an almond inside it, one recites Shehakol. Likewise, over chocolate with nuts one recites Shehakol, for the nuts are secondary to the chocolate (above 8:9). Generally, the name of the food indicates its essence: if it is called a candy or chocolate, the fruit inside it is secondary, and its blessing is Shehakol. And if it is called a coated peanut or chocolate almonds, then the fruit is primary. In any case, even when the sweet is named after the fruit, if a doubt arises – perhaps the coating is thick and it is primary – he should recite Shehakol because of the doubt, for the Shehakol blessing exempts everything.

Ice cream that has pieces of fruit and nuts meant to add flavor to it: the ice cream is primary, and with the Shehakol blessing one exempts the pieces of fruit. Likewise, if a nut was placed on the ice cream, the nut is secondary to the ice cream, and with the Shehakol blessing over the ice cream one exempts the nut. And if, before he began eating the ice cream, he wanted to eat the nut by itself, he recites Ha-etz over it.

Many snack bars nowadays consist of a wafer surrounded by a very thick layer of chocolate. On the one hand it is clear that the main component of the food is the chocolate, and on the other hand, since the wafer is of a grain species, it has importance. According to halakha, the law depends on the purpose of the wafer: usually it is meant to give flavor, and consequently its blessing is Mezonot. But if it is meant only to give the chocolate structure and to create a special crunchy texture for it, then the wafer is secondary, and the blessing over the snack is Shehakol. In practice, the person eating must decide whether the wafer has independent importance, and recite Mezonot, or whether it merely assists and is secondary to the chocolate, and recite Shehakol. One need not be too worried about erring, for either way one fulfills the obligation (Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 208:31. Regarding the after-blessing, he recites Borei Nefashot, unless he knows with certainty that he ate a kezayit of the grain and the grain was important for the taste; see above halakha 4).

sections.title: Soup Containing Several Kinds
sections.html:
The vegetable soup common today is a soup whose main flavor comes from soup powder; therefore the blessing over the liquid in it is Shehakol, and the blessing over the vegetables in it is Ha-adama (above 8:16). If one of them is primary and the other secondary, one recites the blessing over the primary and exempts the secondary. This law divides into three situations:

a) If the great majority of the soup is liquid, and it contains very few vegetables, they are secondary to the soup, and he recites Shehakol over the soup and with its blessing exempts the few vegetables in it (Sha'ar Ha-tziyun 208:27). b) If most of it is liquid and a significant minority is vegetables, even though the vegetables are the minority, since they have importance, there is no primary and secondary here, and one must recite two blessings over the soup: over the vegetables Ha-adama, and over the liquid Shehakol. c) If close to half of the soup is vegetables, to the point that it is clear to him that they are primary and the liquid secondary, he recites Ha-adama over the vegetables and exempts the liquid (MB 202:54; 205:13). Even if, after he finishes the vegetables, a few spoonfuls of liquid still remain, they are secondary to the vegetables and he need not recite a blessing over them separately. Regarding the after-blessing, over a soup that is mainly water he does not recite a blessing, since he did not drink a revi'it of it continuously (as explained above 10:10); and if it contained vegetables and he ate a kezayit of them within akhilat peras, that is, the volume of half an egg within seven minutes (as explained above 10:7), he recites Borei Nefashot over them.

Soup with dumplings (kneidlach): if it contained many dumplings, and usually he eats the soup together with the dumplings, the dumplings are primary, and he recites Mezonot and exempts the soup. And if it contained few dumplings, he recites Mezonot over the dumplings and Shehakol over the soup.

Soup that contains noodles and vegetables that are difficult to isolate: even when the noodles are the minority, since they are a grain species, they are primary, and he recites Mezonot at the outset and Al Ha-miḥya at the end (SA 208:2). But if the soup contained recognizable pieces of vegetable that can be isolated, there is a doubt whether they are considered part of the mixture and secondary to the noodles. To get out of the doubt, he should first recite Mezonot over the noodles and Ha-adama over the vegetables, and only afterward eat both together (as explained above note 4). Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate half an egg's volume of the noodles (within 7 minutes), he recites Al Ha-miḥya. And if he ate half an egg's volume of the vegetables separately, he also recites Borei Nefashot. And if he ate less than half an egg's volume of the noodles but ate half an egg's volume of the vegetables, even if he did not eat them separately, he recites Borei Nefashot.7

Milk or leben into which grain species whose blessing is Mezonot were placed, and they are mixed such that most of the time some of the grain also comes up in the spoon – he recites Mezonot over everything (above halakha 4). But if they are not so mixed, such that he will often eat leben or milk without grain, he recites Mezonot over the grain and Shehakol over the milk. Regarding the after-blessing, if he ate a kezayit of the grain, he recites Al Ha-miḥya and exempts the leben or milk. And if what he ate did not contain a kezayit of grain, but together with the leben there was a kezayit, he recites Borei Nefashot. And if he ate the grain with milk, he recites nothing at the end, for since he ate them with a spoon, it is not possible that he managed to drink a revi'it of the milk within the time that obligates an after-blessing (see above 10:10; and regarding the law of cereal in milk, see above 6:14).
